costRanges.item: Roof waterproofing / deck sealing — overall job
costRanges.range: Free written estimate; cost varies by roof size and sealing method (no dollar total available)
costRanges.source: Newark Quality Roofing (gold pricing.range — no named cost aggregator gathered for waterproofing; dollar costs explicitly NOT available per facts §9 'Banned: exact dollar cost for waterproofing/deck-sealing')

signs: Brown or yellow ceiling and wall stains near the eaves after a winter thaw — meltwater backing under the covering at an unprotected edge, the condition an ice barrier extending at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line resists (IRC R905.1.2).

Icicles and thick ice ridges along the eaves with interior stains at the top-floor walls — an ice dam forcing meltwater under the shingles; the eave zone an ice barrier seals (IRC R905.1.2 as enforced through the NJ Uniform Construction Code).
Damp or rotted decking at a valley or penetration — water passing a failed detail to the deck, the zone a self-adhered ice-and-water membrane seals around fasteners (ASTM D1970).
Asphalt-saturated felt underlayment as the only secondary barrier — leaves the deck water-resistant rather than waterproof; #15/#30 felt meets ASTM D226 as a water-resistant layer, not a sealed one.
Ponding water held on a low-slope roof more than 48 hours after rain — a defect that breaks down the membrane; a flat roof needs at least 1/4 inch per foot of slope to drain (NRCA, ARMA).
An exposed roof deck during a tear-off or re-roof — the window to seal the deck, because a sealed deck cuts water entry into the home by as much as 95% vs. an unsealed deck (IBHS).

technicalFacts.fact: A fully sealed roof deck can cut water entry into the home by as much as 95% compared with an unsealed deck.
technicalFacts.source: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)

technicalFacts.fact: On a 2,000-square-foot unsealed roof stripped of shingles, up to 750 gallons of water per inch of rain can enter the attic (roughly nine bathtubs); an unsealed deck can let up to ~60% of rain on a damaged roof enter.
technicalFacts.source: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), Anne Cope, P.E.

technicalFacts.fact: IBHS-approved sealed-deck methods: a full self-adhering membrane; taped seams over underlayment; two layers of felt; or sealed joints — chosen to match the roof. Liquid-applied or self-adhered membrane is used at low-slope sections and flashing details where most leaks start.

An ice barrier runs from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, and at least 36 inches along the slope on roofs of 8:12 or steeper; the barrier is either two cemented underlayment layers or one self-adhering polymer-modified bitumen sheet.
technicalFacts.source: IRC R905.1.2 (2021 IRC, NJ-enforced via N.J.A.C. 5:23)

technicalFacts.fact: A self-adhered ice-and-water membrane self-seals around fasteners; asphalt-saturated felt (#15/#30) is water-resistant, not waterproof.

Low-slope / flat roofs need positive drainage at the NRCA minimum design slope of 1/4 inch per foot (~2%); ponding water remaining more than 48 hours counts as a defect that accelerates membrane deterioration.
Sealing the deck during a tear-off or re-roof costs less per square foot than standalone access, because the deck sits exposed and the membrane bonds to bare sheathing.
Repair/replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance — no construction permit, inspection, or notice required.
On a commercial building, sealing more than 25% of total roof area in a 12-month period requires a permit.

codes.requirement: Ice barrier from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line (at least 36 inches along the slope on roofs of 8:12 or steeper); two cemented underlayment layers or one self-adhering polymer-modified bitumen sheet. 2021 IRC, enforced in NJ via N.J.A.C. 5:23 (the 2024 IRC dropped the 36-in add-on, but NJ has not adopted it).
Self-adhering polymer-modified bitumen ice-and-water membrane that self-seals around fasteners.
Asphalt-saturated felt (Type I #15, Type II #30) — a water-resistant secondary barrier, not a waterproof sealed layer.
At least 1/4 inch per foot (~2%) positive slope on a low-slope roof so water drains; ponding > 48 hours is a defect (NRCA, ARMA).

Roof-covering repair/replacement on a detached 1- and 2-family dwelling is ordinary maintenance (no permit); sealing/re-covering more than 25% of a commercial roof's total area in 12 months requires a permit.

namedSources: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS)

defabToKill.issue: Invented Essex County climate stat: 'over a single NJ winter with 80+ freeze-thaw cycles.' No freeze-thaw cycle count exists in the gold or fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the cycle count. Describe freeze-thaw/ice-dam stress qualitatively; ground the eave-leak symptom in IRC R905.1.2 (ice barrier to >=24 in inside the wall line).

defabToKill.issue: Invented valley spec: 'ice-and-water shield extending 18 inches on each side of the valley center line.' The gold gives no valley side-distance number.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the grounded fact: a self-adhered ice-and-water membrane runs under the valley metal and around penetrations and self-seals around fasteners (ASTM D1970). Do not state an 18-inch (or any) valley side measurement.

defabToKill.issue: Vapor-barrier / attic-condensation section frames attic moisture as a 'vapor barrier failure' and an indicator that you need roof waterproofing — conflates ventilation/vapor-control with the deck-sealing service and is off-scope.
defabToKill.fix: Keep the deck/eave/valley/low-slope waterproofing symptoms only (the 6 grounded signs). If attic condensation is mentioned, attribute the root cause to attic heat loss / air leakage (Building Science Digest 135 / Univ. of Minnesota Extension), NOT to a missing roof-waterproofing layer, and do not present it as a primary waterproofing-failure sign.

defabToKill.issue: 'Ice dam leaks during winter are the primary indicator' overstates one symptom; and implies ventilation/eave shield as the root fix.
defabToKill.fix: Lead with the strongest grounded answer (eave stains/icicles signal meltwater backing under the covering past an unprotected edge), code-grounded in IRC R905.1.2; keep ice-dam ROOT CAUSE = attic heat loss/air leakage, with the ice barrier as the sealing remedy at the eave zone.

defabToKill.issue: Entire article is built on fabricated, unsourced dollar figures: I&W '$1.50-3.00/sf', code-min coverage '$500-1,500', full-deck '$2,000-5,000', extended coverage '$300-800/plane', synthetic underlayment '$0.15-0.30/sf', felt-to-synthetic upgrade '$100-300', vapor barrier '$0.50-1.50/sf' / '$750-2,250', '$15,000 re-roof', '$1,500 investment'. The fact pack §9 explicitly bans 'exact dollar cost for waterproofing/deck-sealing (none gathered).'
defabToKill.fix: Remove ALL dollar amounts. Reframe the cost answer around free-estimate framing + the gold pricing FACTORS: cost varies by roof size and sealing method (the four IBHS-approved deck-sealing methods each priced by roof area), plus material for ice-barrier eave protection, self-adhered valley/penetration membrane, and low-slope/flashing-detail membrane; sealing the deck during a tear-off/re-roof costs less per sf than standalone access. End with a free written estimate.

defabToKill.issue: Fabricated ROI/percentage statistics: 'prevent 60%+ of water intrusion scenarios', 'waterproofing = 5-15% of total project cost', 'NJ insurance claims for interior water damage average $8,000-12,000 per incident', '$5,000-20,000 ice dam damage events', 'guaranteed payback'.
defabToKill.fix: Drop all of these. The only grounded quantified value is the IBHS finding: a sealed deck cuts water entry into the home by as much as 95% vs. an unsealed deck, and an unsealed 2,000-sf deck can admit up to 750 gallons per inch of rain (~nine bathtubs). Use those IBHS figures instead of invented ROI/claim numbers; never promise 'guaranteed payback.'

defabToKill.issue: Claims 'attic vapor barriers required in NJ when attic ventilation is below 1:150 ratio' as a priced line item — conflates ventilation with the waterproofing service and misstates the code basis.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the vapor-barrier line item from the cost guide (out of scope; no source). If ventilation is referenced at all, design ratio in Newark/Essex (IRC Climate Zone 4-5) is 1:150 (IRC R806.2); do NOT claim Newark qualifies for the 1/300 reduced ratio.

defabToKill.issue: Invented 'best practice' numeric upgrades: 'extending ice-and-water shield to 4-6 feet up from eaves', 'apply ice-and-water shield at all roof-to-wall junctions' — presented as superior-to-code specs with no source.
defabToKill.fix: State the actual code requirement (IRC R905.1.2: eave to >=24 in inside the wall line, >=36 in up-slope on >=8:12 roofs) and the grounded waterproofing zones (deck, eaves, valleys/penetrations per ASTM D1970, low-slope/flashing details on a roof graded to the NRCA 1/4 in/ft minimum). Drop the 4-6 ft and 'all junctions' invented specs.

defabToKill.issue: Off-topic basement/foundation section ('Moisture Management and Your Home's Basement', gutter discharge, downspout extensions, grading) — not part of roof waterproofing and absent from the gold scope.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with on-scope decision content: what roof waterproofing seals (the layer beneath the covering), why it matters (IBHS 95% / 750-gallon figures), the NJ ice-barrier requirement, the best moment to do it (during a tear-off/re-roof when the deck is exposed), the repair-vs-replace thresholds (covering serves its lifespan + localized leak = waterproof/repair; >25-30% area damage or one repair near 50% of replacement = replace, contractor-consensus), and what to verify (registered NJ HIC, insured, manufacturer-approved bonding to keep a system warranty intact).

defabToKill.issue: 'NJ code has progressively strengthened waterproofing requirements' / vague era comparisons ('homes from the 1980s') stated without a code citation.
defabToKill.fix: Anchor the code statement to the specific NJ-enforced sections (IRC R905.1.2 ice barrier; ASTM D1970/D226 membrane vs. felt) under the 2021 IRC adopted via N.J.A.C. 5:23, rather than vague decade comparisons.

defabToKill.issue: Implies NQR holds installer certifications / superior proprietary methods.
defabToKill.fix: NQR's credential = registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (NEVER 'licensed'), insured. NQR applies the IBHS-approved sealing methods and bonds membrane to manufacturer-approved details to keep a system warranty intact; no installer-certification self-claim (brand names like Firestone/Carlisle/Johns Manville as systems NQR installs are fine).

articleAngles.signs: Definitively answer that the signs you need roof waterproofing are eave/edge symptoms of water bypassing the covering and reaching the deck: brown/yellow ceiling-and-wall stains near the eaves after a thaw, icicles/ice ridges at the eaves with top-floor interior stains (ice dam past an unprotected edge), damp or rotted decking at a valley or penetration, ponding held >48 hours on a low-slope roof, felt-only secondary barrier, and an exposed deck at tear-off. Strongest grounded facts: IBHS 95% water-entry reduction; ASTM D1970 self-sealing membrane; IRC R905.1.2 ice barrier (24 in inside wall line); NRCA 1/4 in/ft min slope with ponding >48 h = defect. Ice-dam root cause = attic heat loss/air leakage (not gutters/ventilation).
articleAngles.costGuide: Definitively answer that roof waterproofing has no fixed price — cost varies by roof size and sealing method, so NQR gives a free written estimate. Cite ONLY grounded value figures, not dollar quotes: IBHS — a sealed deck cuts water entry into the home by as much as 95% vs. an unsealed deck, and an unsealed 2,000-sf deck can admit up to 750 gallons per inch of rain (~nine bathtubs). Cost factors (from gold pricing.factors): the four IBHS-approved deck-sealing methods (full self-adhering membrane / taped seams over underlayment / two layers of felt / sealed joints), each priced by roof area; ice-barrier eave material; self-adhered valley/penetration membrane (ASTM D1970); low-slope/flashing-detail membrane on a roof graded to NRCA 1/4 in/ft; and that sealing the deck during a tear-off/re-roof costs less per sf than standalone access. Strip every $ figure and ROI/insurance-claim stat from the old copy.
articleAngles.decision: Definitively answer that roof waterproofing seals the layer beneath the covering (deck, eaves, valleys/penetrations, low-slope/flashing details) so wind-driven rain that gets past shingles/membrane stops at the deck — sealed deck = up to 95% less water entry, unsealed 2,000-sf deck = up to 750 gal/in (IBHS). Cover: how it works (4 zones), why NJ needs it (ice dams from attic heat loss; IRC R905.1.2 ice barrier 24 in inside wall line / 36 in up-slope on >=8:12, enforced via N.J.A.C. 5:23), the best time (during a tear-off/re-roof while the deck is exposed; ordinary-maintenance/no-permit on detached 1-2 family dwellings per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, vs. >25% commercial-area permit), repair-vs-replace thresholds (lifespan + localized leak = waterproof/repair; >25-30% area or one repair ~50% of replacement = replace), and what to verify in a contractor: registered NJ HIC (not 'licensed'), insured, IBHS-approved methods, manufacturer-approved bonding to keep a system warranty intact. Drop the basement/foundation tangent and the invented 4-6 ft / all-junction best-practice specs.
